chapter.title: What it owns: assets, fast and slow

cards.body: The list of assets on a balance sheet is a speed ranking: it sorts things by how fast each one could turn into cash. Walk through the house from our picture. The notes in the kitchen drawer could be spent tonight, but the house itself would take months to sell. **Same house, two speeds of owning.**
cards.simpler: A balance sheet lists what a company owns in order of speed: how fast each thing could turn into cash. Think back to the house in our picture. The notes in the kitchen drawer could be spent tonight. The house itself would take months to sell. **Same house, two speeds of owning.**

cards.prompt: It's Saturday and the boiler has just died. You need £500 by Monday. Which thing you own gets you that cash fastest?

options.text: The £500 your sister owes you and promised to pay back this weekend
The £1,200 sofa you bought last year

whyNot.a: That mixes up what's worth the most with what's fastest. A house is worth more, but selling one takes months.
whyNot.c: That mixes up value with speed. The sofa is worth something, but first you'd have to find a buyer.

cards.reteach: The question is how soon something turns into cash, not how much it's worth. Money someone has promised to pay you this week is almost cash already. A house or a sofa has to be sold first, and selling takes time.

cards.title: Fast: current assets
cards.body:
Accountants split everything a company owns using one rule of thumb: 12 months. Anything expected to turn into cash within a year is a *current asset*. Think of it as the fast pile.

Three lines usually make up most of it. First, cash: the money in the bank. Second, *receivables*: bills customers owe but haven't paid yet, like your sister's £500. Third, *inventory*: the stock on the shelves waiting to be sold.

You'd think cash would be the biggest fast line. In many shops and factories, it's one of the smaller ones. **Fast means it should become cash within a year, not that it's cash already.**
cards.simpler: Accountants sort what a company owns with one rule of thumb: 12 months. Anything expected to become cash within a year is a *current asset*, the fast pile. It's mostly three things: cash in the bank, *receivables* (money customers owe but haven't paid yet, like your sister's £500), and *inventory*, the stock waiting to be sold. In many shops and factories, cash is one of the smaller three. **Fast means it should become cash within a year, not that it's cash already.**

cards.title: Spoke & Co., a made-up bike shop
cards.body: It's 31 December at Spoke & Co. There's £40,000 in the bank. A courier firm still owes £15,000 for six cargo bikes. The shop floor holds £120,000 of bikes, including a purple tandem nobody has wanted since March. That's £175,000 in the fast pile. The slow pile is the workshop building at £300,000 plus £25,000 of tools. **Total: £500,000, and the biggest single thing the shop owns is a building it can't spend.**
cards.simpler: It's 31 December at Spoke & Co. The bank holds £40,000. A courier firm still owes £15,000 for six cargo bikes. The shop floor has £120,000 of bikes, including a purple tandem nobody has wanted since March. That's £175,000 in the fast pile. The slow pile is the workshop building, worth £300,000, plus £25,000 of tools. **Total: £500,000, and the biggest thing the shop owns is a building it can't spend.**

cards.prompt: Spoke & Co. adds three new lines: £9,000 a school owes for bikes delivered last week, a £60,000 van the shop plans to use for six years, and £2,000 of inner tubes in the stockroom. Which sorting is right?

options.text: All three are fast, because each one could be sold
The school's bill and the inner tubes are fast; the van is slow
Only the school's bill is fast; the tubes and the van are physical things, so they're slow

whyNot.a: That's asking what could be sold, not what will turn into cash within 12 months. The van is meant to be driven for years.
whyNot.c: That's sorting by object versus paper, not fast versus slow. The tubes are stock that should sell this year, so they're fast.

cards.reteach: Sort by the plan, not by the object. Ask whether it will become cash, or get used up, within 12 months. The school's bill and the tubes will. The van will be driven for six years, so it goes in the slow pile.

cards.title: Slow: long-term assets
cards.body:
Everything else is a *non-current asset*, the slow pile. These are things the company keeps to do its work, not to sell: buildings, machines, vans, computers. In the house, that's the house itself and the new boiler. You live with them; you don't sell them on a Tuesday.

One odd line sits here too: brands the company bought from someone else. Here's the twist. **A brand a company built itself mostly isn't on the sheet at all, but a brand it bought is.**
cards.simpler: Everything else is a *non-current asset*, the slow pile. These are things a company keeps to do its work, not to sell: buildings, machines, vans, computers. In the house, that's the house itself and the new boiler. Brands bought from someone else sit here too. Oddly, **a brand a company built itself mostly isn't on the sheet at all, but a brand it bought is.**

cards.body: Priya opens a café chain's balance sheet, sees £2 million of assets and decides the company is rolling in money. Then she looks closer: £1.9 million is ovens, counters and shop fittings, and the cash line says £40,000. The total is big, but the fast pile is thin. To spot this, **read 'total current assets' before the grand total**, every time.
cards.simpler: Priya opens a café chain's balance sheet and sees £2 million of assets. She decides the company is rolling in money. Then she looks closer. £1.9 million is ovens, counters and shop fittings, and the cash line says just £40,000. The total is big, but the fast pile is thin. To catch this, **read 'total current assets' before the grand total**, every time.

cards.prompt: A friend says: 'This company has £10 million of assets, so it can easily pay a £1 million bill next month.' What should you ask first?

options.text: How much of the £10 million is fast: cash, customer bills and stock?
Is £10 million more than it had last year?
Does the company own its own brand?

whyNot.b: That's about growth, not speed. Even a bigger pile of buildings can't pay a bill next month.
whyNot.c: That's about what kind of slow asset it has, not how much fast money it has. A brand can't pay next month's bill.

cards.reteach: Next month's bill gets paid from the fast pile, not the total. When the plumber needs paying, you reach for the kitchen drawer, not the deeds to the house. So split the £10 million into fast and slow before deciding anything.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Everything a company owns goes in one of two piles: fast things that should become cash within 12 months (cash, customer bills, stock) and slow things it keeps to do the work (buildings, machines, brands it bought). The total tells you how big the house is; **the fast pile tells you what's in the kitchen drawer.**
cards.simpler: Everything a company owns goes into one of two piles. The fast pile holds things that should become cash within 12 months: cash, customer bills and stock. The slow pile holds things it keeps to do the work: buildings, machines and brands it bought. The total tells you how big the house is. **The fast pile tells you what's in the kitchen drawer.**

cards.body:
Pick a big chain you shopped at this week (big listed companies publish their accounts; many small shops don't). Search its name plus 'balance sheet'. Find two lines, 'total current assets' and 'total assets', and work out roughly what share of everything it owns is fast.

Tomorrow: how a company can owe billions and still be perfectly healthy.
cards.simpler: Pick a big chain you shopped at this week. Big companies usually publish their accounts; many small shops don't. Search its name plus 'balance sheet'. Find two lines: 'total current assets' and 'total assets'. The first is the fast pile. The second is everything the company owns. Compare the two and work out roughly **what share of everything it owns is fast.** Tomorrow: how a company can owe billions and still be perfectly healthy.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now sort every asset line into fast or slow and name the two or three biggest things a company owns.

dubious_claims: 'You'd think cash would be the biggest fast line. Often it's the smallest.' This overreaches. For many cash-rich companies, such as big tech firms, cash is the largest current asset. It only holds reliably for retailers and manufacturers.
'12 months' is presented as the only rule. Strictly, the cutoff is 12 months or the operating cycle, whichever is longer. That is an acceptable simplification, but it is not the full rule.
The try card assumes any shop you used this week publishes a balance sheet. Many private businesses don't, or they file only abbreviated accounts.
Open loop fails on placement: the 'Tomorrow:' teaser is on card 9, but the chapter actually ends on the try card, which has no pull toward the next chapter.
repairedFrom.why: At about 118 words it is the longest teach card, and it packs three separate ideas into one: the slow pile, the bought-brand twist, and US vs international ordering. The ordering point is never tested, and the brand point only shows up as a wrong option.
repairedFrom.fix: Delete the last paragraph about US vs international ordering. That brings the card under 90 words and leaves the brand twist as its only payoff.
